title: BREAKING | Tesla and SpaceX have tapped 5 directors to negotiate a potential $3.5 trillion merger that, if completed, would be the largest in history!
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

The most exciting possibility is what the two companies could build together. Tesla brings experience manufacturing electric vehicles and batteries at scale. SpaceX brings reusable rockets and Starlink, a satellite network that connects customers in places terrestrial networks struggle to reach. Together, they could design products around reliable power, connectivity and automation from the start.

Start with a practical example. A mine, construction site or remote industrial facility might need battery storage, a reliable internet connection and equipment that operators can monitor from miles away. Tesla’s energy storage and Starlink’s connectivity could form the backbone of a package designed for those conditions. Joint engineering could make installation and maintenance easier, particularly for customers operating across dozens of sites. The same approach could help restore power and communications after a disaster, when both are needed quickly.

Manufacturing could be an even bigger opportunity. Tesla has spent years designing products for high-volume production. SpaceX has built its launch business around making complex hardware reusable and improving it through repeated flights. Those are complementary disciplines. The interesting question is where engineers from both companies could redesign a component, a production line or a test process together and measurably improve cost, reliability or speed.

AI is another area to watch. The FT reports that advisers are examining overlap in AI, chip design and data centers. If the companies identify computing needs they genuinely share, they could pool some infrastructure spending and give engineering teams more resources to develop and test software. The payoff would show up in specific outcomes, such as forecasting power demand more accurately or spotting equipment faults earlier.

Why it matters for shareholders. A combined company could fund projects that are hard to pursue when the costs sit with one company and the benefits flow to the other. It could also take a successful product developed for one business and adapt it for customers across the other. To make that opportunity tangible, the boards could lay out the first projects they would fund, what those projects would cost and how investors could track their progress.

Deal terms will matter just as much as the engineering. The committees are exploring an all-stock transaction, so the exchange ratio would determine how much of the combined company each shareholder group owns. Clear voting rights and a board equipped to oversee capital allocation would give investors a stronger basis for backing an ambitious operating plan.

The upside is a business that can take ideas from the lab into factories, onto the grid and into orbit. If the directors can agree on fair terms and identify a few projects that benefit directly from common ownership, shareholders will have something concrete to get excited about. The first sign of success could be as simple as a remote facility getting dependable power and internet from one integrated system.

Sources:
